case_info.explanation: D. Start doxazosin (2 mg twice daily, titrating up as needed to maintain blood pressure control) The key to the correct diagnosis is presence of an elevated normetanephrine concentration in a patient with a retroperitoneal mass. Choice A is not recommended because biopsy can precipitate catecholamine crisis, consisting of a surge of catecholamine release that may cause hypertensive emergency, myocardial infarction, stroke, or aortic dissection. Discontinuing metoprolol succinate (choice B) is incorrect because β-blockers can prevent reflex tachycardia associated with α-1 adrenergic blocker medications, recommended for preoperative management of paragangliomas. Gallium-68 DOTATATE imaging (choice C) is not indicated because additional imaging is not necessary for diagnosis. Tumors of the autonomic nervous system that arise from chromaffin tissue (neural tissue that produces and secretes catecholamines) include pheochromocytomas (located in the adrenal medulla) and paragangliomas (located in sympathetic extra-adrenal ganglia). Paragangliomas are rare (estimated incidence of up to 0.95 cases per 100 000 people annually), and incidence does not differ by sex.1,2Sympathetic paragangliomas usually secrete catecholamines and metanephrines. Parasympathetic paragangliomas, which are typically located in the head and neck region, are usually nonsecretory.3,4 Paragangliomas may be identified as an incidental finding on an imaging study of the abdomen, pelvis, head, neck, or thorax. However, most patients typically experience palpitations, hypertension, anxiety, and/or syncope (due to secretion of epinephrine) or headaches, sweating, and/or persistent hypertension (due to secretion of norepinephrine).5Due to mass effect, head and neck paragangliomas can cause symptoms such as hoarseness and dysphagia, and retroperitoneal paragangliomas may cause local compression symptoms. Both plasma and urine metanephrine tests have more than a 90% sensitivity for diagnosis of paragangliomas. However, plasma metanephrine testing is favored due to ease of collection and higher specificity (79%-98%) compared with 24-hour urine testing (69%-95%).3Metanephrine or normetanephrine concentrations at least 4 times above the upper limit of normal are consistent with diagnosis of paraganglioma. Patients diagnosed with a paraganglioma based on biochemical testing should undergo abdominal CT or MRI imaging, with and without contrast. Nearly all (99%) of paragangliomas have Hounsfield unit density greater than  10 on unenhanced CT scan.6,7Functional imaging using nuclear scans such as gallium-68 DOTATATE positron emission tomography/CT can be helpful to assess for metastases. Ga-DOTATATE is a radiotracer that binds to somatostatin receptors, which are found on paragangliomas. Guidelines recommend germline genetic testing for all patients diagnosed with paraganglioma.8,9Germline gene variants are found in up to 40% of patients with paragangliomas, who have a high prevalence of hereditary syndromes such as von Hippel–Lindau, multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2, neurofibromatosis type 1, and succinate dehydrogenase gene (SDHx) variant–related tumors.8Identifying a genetic germline variant can help guide management, including surveillance for associated tumors (such as kidney cancer and gastrointestinal stromal tumor in patients withSDHxgene variants) and screening of first-degree family members. First-line treatment of paraganglioma is surgical resection. Prior to surgery, most patients with paraganglioma, and especially those with elevated catecholamine levels, should be treated with an α-adrenergic blocker medication with the nonselective α-1/2–adrenoceptor blocker (phenoxybenzamine) or a selective competitive α-1–adrenoceptor blocker (doxazosin, prazosin, terazosin). These medications prevent excessive vasoconstriction and severe hypertension caused by catecholamine release from the tumor.10β-Adrenergic blockers may be added to treat tachycardia but only after adequate α blockade has been achieved, because unopposed α receptor stimulation may precipitate hypertensive crisis. To assess for recurrence, all patients with paraganglioma should undergo plasma metanephrine and catecholamine testing within 2 months of surgical resection, with repeat testing every 6 to 12 months depending on the risk of recurrence. Patients withSDHBgermline gene variants are recommended to undergo annual biochemical screening with plasma metanephrines and catecholamines and biennial whole-body MRI imaging. The patient was treated with doxazosin (4 mg twice daily), and metoprolol succinate was increased to 50 mg twice daily. Three weeks after presentation, open resection of the paraganglioma was performed, and histological examination confirmed the diagnosis of paraganglioma. After surgery, her palpitations and fatigue resolved, and her migraines slowly improved, resolving after about 1 year. She underwent testing using a panel of 12 genes associated with hereditary paraganglioma, which revealed a pathogenic variant in theSDHBgene. Annual plasma metanephrine concentrations have been normal, and MRI imaging of the neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis has not identified any lesions, with the most recent scan performed 6 years after presentation.

case_info.caption: Abdominal magnetic resonance imaging scan showing a 4.0 × 3.5–cm mass in the patient’s left infrarenal para-aortic region (arrowhead).
case_info.explanation: D. Start doxazosin (2 mg twice daily, titrating up as needed to maintain blood pressure control) The key to the correct diagnosis is presence of an elevated normetanephrine concentration in a patient with a retroperitoneal mass. Choice A is not recommended because biopsy can precipitate catecholamine crisis, consisting of a surge of catecholamine release that may cause hypertensive emergency, myocardial infarction, stroke, or aortic dissection. Discontinuing metoprolol succinate (choice B) is incorrect because β-blockers can prevent reflex tachycardia associated with α-1 adrenergic blocker medications, recommended for preoperative management of paragangliomas. Gallium-68 DOTATATE imaging (choice C) is not indicated because additional imaging is not necessary for diagnosis. Tumors of the autonomic nervous system that arise from chromaffin tissue (neural tissue that produces and secretes catecholamines) include pheochromocytomas (located in the adrenal medulla) and paragangliomas (located in sympathetic extra-adrenal ganglia). Paragangliomas are rare (estimated incidence of up to 0.95 cases per 100 000 people annually), and incidence does not differ by sex.1,2Sympathetic paragangliomas usually secrete catecholamines and metanephrines. Parasympathetic paragangliomas, which are typically located in the head and neck region, are usually nonsecretory.3,4 Paragangliomas may be identified as an incidental finding on an imaging study of the abdomen, pelvis, head, neck, or thorax. However, most patients typically experience palpitations, hypertension, anxiety, and/or syncope (due to secretion of epinephrine) or headaches, sweating, and/or persistent hypertension (due to secretion of norepinephrine).5Due to mass effect, head and neck paragangliomas can cause symptoms such as hoarseness and dysphagia, and retroperitoneal paragangliomas may cause local compression symptoms. Both plasma and urine metanephrine tests have more than a 90% sensitivity for diagnosis of paragangliomas. However, plasma metanephrine testing is favored due to ease of collection and higher specificity (79%-98%) compared with 24-hour urine testing (69%-95%).3Metanephrine or normetanephrine concentrations at least 4 times above the upper limit of normal are consistent with diagnosis of paraganglioma. Patients diagnosed with a paraganglioma based on biochemical testing should undergo abdominal CT or MRI imaging, with and without contrast. Nearly all (99%) of paragangliomas have Hounsfield unit density greater than  10 on unenhanced CT scan.6,7Functional imaging using nuclear scans such as gallium-68 DOTATATE positron emission tomography/CT can be helpful to assess for metastases. Ga-DOTATATE is a radiotracer that binds to somatostatin receptors, which are found on paragangliomas. Guidelines recommend germline genetic testing for all patients diagnosed with paraganglioma.8,9Germline gene variants are found in up to 40% of patients with paragangliomas, who have a high prevalence of hereditary syndromes such as von Hippel–Lindau, multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2, neurofibromatosis type 1, and succinate dehydrogenase gene (SDHx) variant–related tumors.8Identifying a genetic germline variant can help guide management, including surveillance for associated tumors (such as kidney cancer and gastrointestinal stromal tumor in patients withSDHxgene variants) and screening of first-degree family members. First-line treatment of paraganglioma is surgical resection. Prior to surgery, most patients with paraganglioma, and especially those with elevated catecholamine levels, should be treated with an α-adrenergic blocker medication with the nonselective α-1/2–adrenoceptor blocker (phenoxybenzamine) or a selective competitive α-1–adrenoceptor blocker (doxazosin, prazosin, terazosin). These medications prevent excessive vasoconstriction and severe hypertension caused by catecholamine release from the tumor.10β-Adrenergic blockers may be added to treat tachycardia but only after adequate α blockade has been achieved, because unopposed α receptor stimulation may precipitate hypertensive crisis. To assess for recurrence, all patients with paraganglioma should undergo plasma metanephrine and catecholamine testing within 2 months of surgical resection, with repeat testing every 6 to 12 months depending on the risk of recurrence. Patients withSDHBgermline gene variants are recommended to undergo annual biochemical screening with plasma metanephrines and catecholamines and biennial whole-body MRI imaging. The patient was treated with doxazosin (4 mg twice daily), and metoprolol succinate was increased to 50 mg twice daily. Three weeks after presentation, open resection of the paraganglioma was performed, and histological examination confirmed the diagnosis of paraganglioma. After surgery, her palpitations and fatigue resolved, and her migraines slowly improved, resolving after about 1 year. She underwent testing using a panel of 12 genes associated with hereditary paraganglioma, which revealed a pathogenic variant in theSDHBgene. Annual plasma metanephrine concentrations have been normal, and MRI imaging of the neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis has not identified any lesions, with the most recent scan performed 6 years after presentation.

You are a deliberation POLICY steering a conversation between a medical AI and a clinician toward
the best decision, at the lowest cognitive cost to the clinician. You control HOW the AI speaks,
never WHAT the medical answer is (that is the AI's job). Each turn you choose ONE control stage and
write a short guidance instruction for the AI's next utterance.

The 3 control stages (pick exactly one, and only from the reachable list you are given):

- EXPAND  — cheap, safe, broadens the picture. Elicit the clinician's reasoning, ask them to
            justify, or surface a missing goal/criterion/perspective. Do NOT yet evaluate or push
            an option. Effect is often delayed (sets up a later CHALLENGE). Use when the state is
            unclear or the clinician hasn't exposed their rationale.
- CHALLENGE — expensive and highest-yield, but also most likely to make the clinician regress.
            Directly evaluate the option on the table against a goal/criterion, or contrast two
            options, and press the clinician to engage the mismatch. Spend it deliberately: when
            you have reason to think the clinician's current position is wrong or under-examined.
- CONVERGE — cheap, terminal. Recommend the now-best-supported option and invite accept/reject,
            or confirm an agreement already reached. This is the STOP / pacing lever — stop
            spending burden once belief has settled.

Output STRICT JSON only:

  "stage": "EXPAND | CHALLENGE | CONVERGE",
  "reason": "one short sentence: the hidden state you infer and why this stage now",

case_info.explanation: D. Start doxazosin (2 mg twice daily, titrating up as needed to maintain blood pressure control) The key to the correct diagnosis is presence of an elevated normetanephrine concentration in a patient with a retroperitoneal mass. Choice A is not recommended because biopsy can precipitate catecholamine crisis, consisting of a surge of catecholamine release that may cause hypertensive emergency, myocardial infarction, stroke, or aortic dissection. Discontinuing metoprolol succinate (choice B) is incorrect because β-blockers can prevent reflex tachycardia associated with α-1 adrenergic blocker medications, recommended for preoperative management of paragangliomas. Gallium-68 DOTATATE imaging (choice C) is not indicated because additional imaging is not necessary for diagnosis. Tumors of the autonomic nervous system that arise from chromaffin tissue (neural tissue that produces and secretes catecholamines) include pheochromocytomas (located in the adrenal medulla) and paragangliomas (located in sympathetic extra-adrenal ganglia). Paragangliomas are rare (estimated incidence of up to 0.95 cases per 100 000 people annually), and incidence does not differ by sex.1,2Sympathetic paragangliomas usually secrete catecholamines and metanephrines. Parasympathetic paragangliomas, which are typically located in the head and neck region, are usually nonsecretory.3,4 Paragangliomas may be identified as an incidental finding on an imaging study of the abdomen, pelvis, head, neck, or thorax. However, most patients typically experience palpitations, hypertension, anxiety, and/or syncope (due to secretion of epinephrine) or headaches, sweating, and/or persistent hypertension (due to secretion of norepinephrine).5Due to mass effect, head and neck paragangliomas can cause symptoms such as hoarseness and dysphagia, and retroperitoneal paragangliomas may cause local compression symptoms. Both plasma and urine metanephrine tests have more than a 90% sensitivity for diagnosis of paragangliomas. However, plasma metanephrine testing is favored due to ease of collection and higher specificity (79%-98%) compared with 24-hour urine testing (69%-95%).3Metanephrine or normetanephrine concentrations at least 4 times above the upper limit of normal are consistent with diagnosis of paraganglioma. Patients diagnosed with a paraganglioma based on biochemical testing should undergo abdominal CT or MRI imaging, with and without contrast. Nearly all (99%) of paragangliomas have Hounsfield unit density greater than  10 on unenhanced CT scan.6,7Functional imaging using nuclear scans such as gallium-68 DOTATATE positron emission tomography/CT can be helpful to assess for metastases. Ga-DOTATATE is a radiotracer that binds to somatostatin receptors, which are found on paragangliomas. Guidelines recommend germline genetic testing for all patients diagnosed with paraganglioma.8,9Germline gene variants are found in up to 40% of patients with paragangliomas, who have a high prevalence of hereditary syndromes such as von Hippel–Lindau, multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2, neurofibromatosis type 1, and succinate dehydrogenase gene (SDHx) variant–related tumors.8Identifying a genetic germline variant can help guide management, including surveillance for associated tumors (such as kidney cancer and gastrointestinal stromal tumor in patients withSDHxgene variants) and screening of first-degree family members. First-line treatment of paraganglioma is surgical resection. Prior to surgery, most patients with paraganglioma, and especially those with elevated catecholamine levels, should be treated with an α-adrenergic blocker medication with the nonselective α-1/2–adrenoceptor blocker (phenoxybenzamine) or a selective competitive α-1–adrenoceptor blocker (doxazosin, prazosin, terazosin). These medications prevent excessive vasoconstriction and severe hypertension caused by catecholamine release from the tumor.10β-Adrenergic blockers may be added to treat tachycardia but only after adequate α blockade has been achieved, because unopposed α receptor stimulation may precipitate hypertensive crisis. To assess for recurrence, all patients with paraganglioma should undergo plasma metanephrine and catecholamine testing within 2 months of surgical resection, with repeat testing every 6 to 12 months depending on the risk of recurrence. Patients withSDHBgermline gene variants are recommended to undergo annual biochemical screening with plasma metanephrines and catecholamines and biennial whole-body MRI imaging. The patient was treated with doxazosin (4 mg twice daily), and metoprolol succinate was increased to 50 mg twice daily. Three weeks after presentation, open resection of the paraganglioma was performed, and histological examination confirmed the diagnosis of paraganglioma. After surgery, her palpitations and fatigue resolved, and her migraines slowly improved, resolving after about 1 year. She underwent testing using a panel of 12 genes associated with hereditary paraganglioma, which revealed a pathogenic variant in theSDHBgene. Annual plasma metanephrine concentrations have been normal, and MRI imaging of the neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis has not identified any lesions, with the most recent scan performed 6 years after presentation.

   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."

   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI

   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.

       competing options already qualifies.

case_info.caption: Abdominal magnetic resonance imaging scan showing a 4.0 × 3.5–cm mass in the patient’s left infrarenal para-aortic region (arrowhead).
case_info.explanation: D. Start doxazosin (2 mg twice daily, titrating up as needed to maintain blood pressure control) The key to the correct diagnosis is presence of an elevated normetanephrine concentration in a patient with a retroperitoneal mass. Choice A is not recommended because biopsy can precipitate catecholamine crisis, consisting of a surge of catecholamine release that may cause hypertensive emergency, myocardial infarction, stroke, or aortic dissection. Discontinuing metoprolol succinate (choice B) is incorrect because β-blockers can prevent reflex tachycardia associated with α-1 adrenergic blocker medications, recommended for preoperative management of paragangliomas. Gallium-68 DOTATATE imaging (choice C) is not indicated because additional imaging is not necessary for diagnosis. Tumors of the autonomic nervous system that arise from chromaffin tissue (neural tissue that produces and secretes catecholamines) include pheochromocytomas (located in the adrenal medulla) and paragangliomas (located in sympathetic extra-adrenal ganglia). Paragangliomas are rare (estimated incidence of up to 0.95 cases per 100 000 people annually), and incidence does not differ by sex.1,2Sympathetic paragangliomas usually secrete catecholamines and metanephrines. Parasympathetic paragangliomas, which are typically located in the head and neck region, are usually nonsecretory.3,4 Paragangliomas may be identified as an incidental finding on an imaging study of the abdomen, pelvis, head, neck, or thorax. However, most patients typically experience palpitations, hypertension, anxiety, and/or syncope (due to secretion of epinephrine) or headaches, sweating, and/or persistent hypertension (due to secretion of norepinephrine).5Due to mass effect, head and neck paragangliomas can cause symptoms such as hoarseness and dysphagia, and retroperitoneal paragangliomas may cause local compression symptoms. Both plasma and urine metanephrine tests have more than a 90% sensitivity for diagnosis of paragangliomas. However, plasma metanephrine testing is favored due to ease of collection and higher specificity (79%-98%) compared with 24-hour urine testing (69%-95%).3Metanephrine or normetanephrine concentrations at least 4 times above the upper limit of normal are consistent with diagnosis of paraganglioma. Patients diagnosed with a paraganglioma based on biochemical testing should undergo abdominal CT or MRI imaging, with and without contrast. Nearly all (99%) of paragangliomas have Hounsfield unit density greater than  10 on unenhanced CT scan.6,7Functional imaging using nuclear scans such as gallium-68 DOTATATE positron emission tomography/CT can be helpful to assess for metastases. Ga-DOTATATE is a radiotracer that binds to somatostatin receptors, which are found on paragangliomas. Guidelines recommend germline genetic testing for all patients diagnosed with paraganglioma.8,9Germline gene variants are found in up to 40% of patients with paragangliomas, who have a high prevalence of hereditary syndromes such as von Hippel–Lindau, multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2, neurofibromatosis type 1, and succinate dehydrogenase gene (SDHx) variant–related tumors.8Identifying a genetic germline variant can help guide management, including surveillance for associated tumors (such as kidney cancer and gastrointestinal stromal tumor in patients withSDHxgene variants) and screening of first-degree family members. First-line treatment of paraganglioma is surgical resection. Prior to surgery, most patients with paraganglioma, and especially those with elevated catecholamine levels, should be treated with an α-adrenergic blocker medication with the nonselective α-1/2–adrenoceptor blocker (phenoxybenzamine) or a selective competitive α-1–adrenoceptor blocker (doxazosin, prazosin, terazosin). These medications prevent excessive vasoconstriction and severe hypertension caused by catecholamine release from the tumor.10β-Adrenergic blockers may be added to treat tachycardia but only after adequate α blockade has been achieved, because unopposed α receptor stimulation may precipitate hypertensive crisis. To assess for recurrence, all patients with paraganglioma should undergo plasma metanephrine and catecholamine testing within 2 months of surgical resection, with repeat testing every 6 to 12 months depending on the risk of recurrence. Patients withSDHBgermline gene variants are recommended to undergo annual biochemical screening with plasma metanephrines and catecholamines and biennial whole-body MRI imaging. The patient was treated with doxazosin (4 mg twice daily), and metoprolol succinate was increased to 50 mg twice daily. Three weeks after presentation, open resection of the paraganglioma was performed, and histological examination confirmed the diagnosis of paraganglioma. After surgery, her palpitations and fatigue resolved, and her migraines slowly improved, resolving after about 1 year. She underwent testing using a panel of 12 genes associated with hereditary paraganglioma, which revealed a pathogenic variant in theSDHBgene. Annual plasma metanephrine concentrations have been normal, and MRI imaging of the neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis has not identified any lesions, with the most recent scan performed 6 years after presentation.

case_info.caption: Abdominal magnetic resonance imaging scan showing a 4.0 × 3.5–cm mass in the patient’s left infrarenal para-aortic region (arrowhead).
case_info.explanation: D. Start doxazosin (2 mg twice daily, titrating up as needed to maintain blood pressure control) The key to the correct diagnosis is presence of an elevated normetanephrine concentration in a patient with a retroperitoneal mass. Choice A is not recommended because biopsy can precipitate catecholamine crisis, consisting of a surge of catecholamine release that may cause hypertensive emergency, myocardial infarction, stroke, or aortic dissection. Discontinuing metoprolol succinate (choice B) is incorrect because β-blockers can prevent reflex tachycardia associated with α-1 adrenergic blocker medications, recommended for preoperative management of paragangliomas. Gallium-68 DOTATATE imaging (choice C) is not indicated because additional imaging is not necessary for diagnosis. Tumors of the autonomic nervous system that arise from chromaffin tissue (neural tissue that produces and secretes catecholamines) include pheochromocytomas (located in the adrenal medulla) and paragangliomas (located in sympathetic extra-adrenal ganglia). Paragangliomas are rare (estimated incidence of up to 0.95 cases per 100 000 people annually), and incidence does not differ by sex.1,2Sympathetic paragangliomas usually secrete catecholamines and metanephrines. Parasympathetic paragangliomas, which are typically located in the head and neck region, are usually nonsecretory.3,4 Paragangliomas may be identified as an incidental finding on an imaging study of the abdomen, pelvis, head, neck, or thorax. However, most patients typically experience palpitations, hypertension, anxiety, and/or syncope (due to secretion of epinephrine) or headaches, sweating, and/or persistent hypertension (due to secretion of norepinephrine).5Due to mass effect, head and neck paragangliomas can cause symptoms such as hoarseness and dysphagia, and retroperitoneal paragangliomas may cause local compression symptoms. Both plasma and urine metanephrine tests have more than a 90% sensitivity for diagnosis of paragangliomas. However, plasma metanephrine testing is favored due to ease of collection and higher specificity (79%-98%) compared with 24-hour urine testing (69%-95%).3Metanephrine or normetanephrine concentrations at least 4 times above the upper limit of normal are consistent with diagnosis of paraganglioma. Patients diagnosed with a paraganglioma based on biochemical testing should undergo abdominal CT or MRI imaging, with and without contrast. Nearly all (99%) of paragangliomas have Hounsfield unit density greater than  10 on unenhanced CT scan.6,7Functional imaging using nuclear scans such as gallium-68 DOTATATE positron emission tomography/CT can be helpful to assess for metastases. Ga-DOTATATE is a radiotracer that binds to somatostatin receptors, which are found on paragangliomas. Guidelines recommend germline genetic testing for all patients diagnosed with paraganglioma.8,9Germline gene variants are found in up to 40% of patients with paragangliomas, who have a high prevalence of hereditary syndromes such as von Hippel–Lindau, multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2, neurofibromatosis type 1, and succinate dehydrogenase gene (SDHx) variant–related tumors.8Identifying a genetic germline variant can help guide management, including surveillance for associated tumors (such as kidney cancer and gastrointestinal stromal tumor in patients withSDHxgene variants) and screening of first-degree family members. First-line treatment of paraganglioma is surgical resection. Prior to surgery, most patients with paraganglioma, and especially those with elevated catecholamine levels, should be treated with an α-adrenergic blocker medication with the nonselective α-1/2–adrenoceptor blocker (phenoxybenzamine) or a selective competitive α-1–adrenoceptor blocker (doxazosin, prazosin, terazosin). These medications prevent excessive vasoconstriction and severe hypertension caused by catecholamine release from the tumor.10β-Adrenergic blockers may be added to treat tachycardia but only after adequate α blockade has been achieved, because unopposed α receptor stimulation may precipitate hypertensive crisis. To assess for recurrence, all patients with paraganglioma should undergo plasma metanephrine and catecholamine testing within 2 months of surgical resection, with repeat testing every 6 to 12 months depending on the risk of recurrence. Patients withSDHBgermline gene variants are recommended to undergo annual biochemical screening with plasma metanephrines and catecholamines and biennial whole-body MRI imaging. The patient was treated with doxazosin (4 mg twice daily), and metoprolol succinate was increased to 50 mg twice daily. Three weeks after presentation, open resection of the paraganglioma was performed, and histological examination confirmed the diagnosis of paraganglioma. After surgery, her palpitations and fatigue resolved, and her migraines slowly improved, resolving after about 1 year. She underwent testing using a panel of 12 genes associated with hereditary paraganglioma, which revealed a pathogenic variant in theSDHBgene. Annual plasma metanephrine concentrations have been normal, and MRI imaging of the neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis has not identified any lesions, with the most recent scan performed 6 years after presentation.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.answer: Start doxazosin (2 mg twice daily, titrating up as needed to maintain blood pressure control)
case_info.caption: Abdominal magnetic resonance imaging scan showing a 4.0 × 3.5–cm mass in the patient’s left infrarenal para-aortic region (arrowhead).
case_info.explanation: D. Start doxazosin (2 mg twice daily, titrating up as needed to maintain blood pressure control) The key to the correct diagnosis is presence of an elevated normetanephrine concentration in a patient with a retroperitoneal mass. Choice A is not recommended because biopsy can precipitate catecholamine crisis, consisting of a surge of catecholamine release that may cause hypertensive emergency, myocardial infarction, stroke, or aortic dissection. Discontinuing metoprolol succinate (choice B) is incorrect because β-blockers can prevent reflex tachycardia associated with α-1 adrenergic blocker medications, recommended for preoperative management of paragangliomas. Gallium-68 DOTATATE imaging (choice C) is not indicated because additional imaging is not necessary for diagnosis. Tumors of the autonomic nervous system that arise from chromaffin tissue (neural tissue that produces and secretes catecholamines) include pheochromocytomas (located in the adrenal medulla) and paragangliomas (located in sympathetic extra-adrenal ganglia). Paragangliomas are rare (estimated incidence of up to 0.95 cases per 100 000 people annually), and incidence does not differ by sex.1,2Sympathetic paragangliomas usually secrete catecholamines and metanephrines. Parasympathetic paragangliomas, which are typically located in the head and neck region, are usually nonsecretory.3,4 Paragangliomas may be identified as an incidental finding on an imaging study of the abdomen, pelvis, head, neck, or thorax. However, most patients typically experience palpitations, hypertension, anxiety, and/or syncope (due to secretion of epinephrine) or headaches, sweating, and/or persistent hypertension (due to secretion of norepinephrine).5Due to mass effect, head and neck paragangliomas can cause symptoms such as hoarseness and dysphagia, and retroperitoneal paragangliomas may cause local compression symptoms. Both plasma and urine metanephrine tests have more than a 90% sensitivity for diagnosis of paragangliomas. However, plasma metanephrine testing is favored due to ease of collection and higher specificity (79%-98%) compared with 24-hour urine testing (69%-95%).3Metanephrine or normetanephrine concentrations at least 4 times above the upper limit of normal are consistent with diagnosis of paraganglioma. Patients diagnosed with a paraganglioma based on biochemical testing should undergo abdominal CT or MRI imaging, with and without contrast. Nearly all (99%) of paragangliomas have Hounsfield unit density greater than  10 on unenhanced CT scan.6,7Functional imaging using nuclear scans such as gallium-68 DOTATATE positron emission tomography/CT can be helpful to assess for metastases. Ga-DOTATATE is a radiotracer that binds to somatostatin receptors, which are found on paragangliomas. Guidelines recommend germline genetic testing for all patients diagnosed with paraganglioma.8,9Germline gene variants are found in up to 40% of patients with paragangliomas, who have a high prevalence of hereditary syndromes such as von Hippel–Lindau, multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2, neurofibromatosis type 1, and succinate dehydrogenase gene (SDHx) variant–related tumors.8Identifying a genetic germline variant can help guide management, including surveillance for associated tumors (such as kidney cancer and gastrointestinal stromal tumor in patients withSDHxgene variants) and screening of first-degree family members. First-line treatment of paraganglioma is surgical resection. Prior to surgery, most patients with paraganglioma, and especially those with elevated catecholamine levels, should be treated with an α-adrenergic blocker medication with the nonselective α-1/2–adrenoceptor blocker (phenoxybenzamine) or a selective competitive α-1–adrenoceptor blocker (doxazosin, prazosin, terazosin). These medications prevent excessive vasoconstriction and severe hypertension caused by catecholamine release from the tumor.10β-Adrenergic blockers may be added to treat tachycardia but only after adequate α blockade has been achieved, because unopposed α receptor stimulation may precipitate hypertensive crisis. To assess for recurrence, all patients with paraganglioma should undergo plasma metanephrine and catecholamine testing within 2 months of surgical resection, with repeat testing every 6 to 12 months depending on the risk of recurrence. Patients withSDHBgermline gene variants are recommended to undergo annual biochemical screening with plasma metanephrines and catecholamines and biennial whole-body MRI imaging. The patient was treated with doxazosin (4 mg twice daily), and metoprolol succinate was increased to 50 mg twice daily. Three weeks after presentation, open resection of the paraganglioma was performed, and histological examination confirmed the diagnosis of paraganglioma. After surgery, her palpitations and fatigue resolved, and her migraines slowly improved, resolving after about 1 year. She underwent testing using a panel of 12 genes associated with hereditary paraganglioma, which revealed a pathogenic variant in theSDHBgene. Annual plasma metanephrine concentrations have been normal, and MRI imaging of the neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis has not identified any lesions, with the most recent scan performed 6 years after presentation.

            or confirm an agreement already reached. This is the STOP / pacing lever — stop

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.caption: Abdominal magnetic resonance imaging scan showing a 4.0 × 3.5–cm mass in the patient’s left infrarenal para-aortic region (arrowhead).
case_info.explanation: D. Start doxazosin (2 mg twice daily, titrating up as needed to maintain blood pressure control) The key to the correct diagnosis is presence of an elevated normetanephrine concentration in a patient with a retroperitoneal mass. Choice A is not recommended because biopsy can precipitate catecholamine crisis, consisting of a surge of catecholamine release that may cause hypertensive emergency, myocardial infarction, stroke, or aortic dissection. Discontinuing metoprolol succinate (choice B) is incorrect because β-blockers can prevent reflex tachycardia associated with α-1 adrenergic blocker medications, recommended for preoperative management of paragangliomas. Gallium-68 DOTATATE imaging (choice C) is not indicated because additional imaging is not necessary for diagnosis. Tumors of the autonomic nervous system that arise from chromaffin tissue (neural tissue that produces and secretes catecholamines) include pheochromocytomas (located in the adrenal medulla) and paragangliomas (located in sympathetic extra-adrenal ganglia). Paragangliomas are rare (estimated incidence of up to 0.95 cases per 100 000 people annually), and incidence does not differ by sex.1,2Sympathetic paragangliomas usually secrete catecholamines and metanephrines. Parasympathetic paragangliomas, which are typically located in the head and neck region, are usually nonsecretory.3,4 Paragangliomas may be identified as an incidental finding on an imaging study of the abdomen, pelvis, head, neck, or thorax. However, most patients typically experience palpitations, hypertension, anxiety, and/or syncope (due to secretion of epinephrine) or headaches, sweating, and/or persistent hypertension (due to secretion of norepinephrine).5Due to mass effect, head and neck paragangliomas can cause symptoms such as hoarseness and dysphagia, and retroperitoneal paragangliomas may cause local compression symptoms. Both plasma and urine metanephrine tests have more than a 90% sensitivity for diagnosis of paragangliomas. However, plasma metanephrine testing is favored due to ease of collection and higher specificity (79%-98%) compared with 24-hour urine testing (69%-95%).3Metanephrine or normetanephrine concentrations at least 4 times above the upper limit of normal are consistent with diagnosis of paraganglioma. Patients diagnosed with a paraganglioma based on biochemical testing should undergo abdominal CT or MRI imaging, with and without contrast. Nearly all (99%) of paragangliomas have Hounsfield unit density greater than  10 on unenhanced CT scan.6,7Functional imaging using nuclear scans such as gallium-68 DOTATATE positron emission tomography/CT can be helpful to assess for metastases. Ga-DOTATATE is a radiotracer that binds to somatostatin receptors, which are found on paragangliomas. Guidelines recommend germline genetic testing for all patients diagnosed with paraganglioma.8,9Germline gene variants are found in up to 40% of patients with paragangliomas, who have a high prevalence of hereditary syndromes such as von Hippel–Lindau, multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2, neurofibromatosis type 1, and succinate dehydrogenase gene (SDHx) variant–related tumors.8Identifying a genetic germline variant can help guide management, including surveillance for associated tumors (such as kidney cancer and gastrointestinal stromal tumor in patients withSDHxgene variants) and screening of first-degree family members. First-line treatment of paraganglioma is surgical resection. Prior to surgery, most patients with paraganglioma, and especially those with elevated catecholamine levels, should be treated with an α-adrenergic blocker medication with the nonselective α-1/2–adrenoceptor blocker (phenoxybenzamine) or a selective competitive α-1–adrenoceptor blocker (doxazosin, prazosin, terazosin). These medications prevent excessive vasoconstriction and severe hypertension caused by catecholamine release from the tumor.10β-Adrenergic blockers may be added to treat tachycardia but only after adequate α blockade has been achieved, because unopposed α receptor stimulation may precipitate hypertensive crisis. To assess for recurrence, all patients with paraganglioma should undergo plasma metanephrine and catecholamine testing within 2 months of surgical resection, with repeat testing every 6 to 12 months depending on the risk of recurrence. Patients withSDHBgermline gene variants are recommended to undergo annual biochemical screening with plasma metanephrines and catecholamines and biennial whole-body MRI imaging. The patient was treated with doxazosin (4 mg twice daily), and metoprolol succinate was increased to 50 mg twice daily. Three weeks after presentation, open resection of the paraganglioma was performed, and histological examination confirmed the diagnosis of paraganglioma. After surgery, her palpitations and fatigue resolved, and her migraines slowly improved, resolving after about 1 year. She underwent testing using a panel of 12 genes associated with hereditary paraganglioma, which revealed a pathogenic variant in theSDHBgene. Annual plasma metanephrine concentrations have been normal, and MRI imaging of the neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis has not identified any lesions, with the most recent scan performed 6 years after presentation.

Tumors of the autonomic nervous system that arise from chromaffin tissue (neural tissue that produces and secretes catecholamines) include pheochromocytomas (located in the adrenal medulla) and paragangliomas (located in sympathetic extra-adrenal ganglia). Paragangliomas are rare (estimated incidence of up to 0.95 cases per 100 000 people annually), and incidence does not differ by sex.1,2Sympathetic paragangliomas usually secrete catecholamines and metanephrines. Parasympathetic paragangliomas, which are typically located in the head and neck region, are usually nonsecretory.3,4 Paragangliomas may be identified as an incidental finding on an imaging study of the abdomen, pelvis, head, neck, or thorax. However, most patients typically experience palpitations, hypertension, anxiety, and/or syncope (due to secretion of epinephrine) or headaches, sweating, and/or persistent hypertension (due to secretion of norepinephrine).5Due to mass effect, head and neck paragangliomas can cause symptoms such as hoarseness and dysphagia, and retroperitoneal paragangliomas may cause local compression symptoms. Both plasma and urine metanephrine tests have more than a 90% sensitivity for diagnosis of paragangliomas. However, plasma metanephrine testing is favored due to ease of collection and higher specificity (79%-98%) compared with 24-hour urine testing (69%-95%).3Metanephrine or normetanephrine concentrations at least 4 times above the upper limit of normal are consistent with diagnosis of paraganglioma. Ga-DOTATATE is a radiotracer that binds to somatostatin receptors, which are found on paragangliomas. Guidelines recommend germline genetic testing for all patients diagnosed with paraganglioma.8,9Germline gene variants are found in up to 40% of patients with paragangliomas, who have a high prevalence of hereditary syndromes such as von Hippel–Lindau, multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2, neurofibromatosis type 1, and succinate dehydrogenase gene (SDHx) variant–related tumors.8Identifying a genetic germline variant can help guide management, including surveillance for associated tumors (such as kidney cancer and gastrointestinal stromal tumor in patients withSDHxgene variants) and screening of first-degree family members. First-line treatment of paraganglioma is surgical resection. Prior to surgery, most patients with paraganglioma, and especially those with elevated catecholamine levels, should be treated with an α-adrenergic blocker medication with the nonselective α-1/2–adrenoceptor blocker (phenoxybenzamine) or a selective competitive α-1–adrenoceptor blocker (doxazosin, prazosin, terazosin).
